content: Floaters are small deposits of varying size, shape, consistency, refractive index, and motility that exist within the normally transparent vitreous humor of the eye. These deposits can originate from embryonic remnants or develop later due to degenerative changes in the vitreous humor or retina. The perception of floaters is medically referred to as myodesopsia, or less commonly as myiodeopsia. Subjectively, floaters are entoptic phenomena, meaning they are visual disturbances caused by structures within the eye itself. They appear as shadow-like shapes in the visual field, often described as spots, threads, or cobweb-like fragments that drift slowly across the field of vision. A specific type of floater, known as muscae volitantes (Latin for flying flies), consists of small spots that are considered normal and are attributed to minute remnants of embryonic structures within the vitreous humor. Floaters are suspended in the vitreous humor, a gel-like substance that fills the eye. They tend to follow the rapid movements of the eye but drift slowly within the fluid. When first noticed, individuals often attempt to look directly at them, but this is challenging because floaters move with the motion of the eye, remaining just out of direct focus. Floaters are visible because they are not fixed in position within the eye, unlike the blood vessels of the retina, which are stabilized and tuned out by the brain through neural adaptation. Floaters are particularly noticeable when looking at a blank surface or a uniformly lit background, such as a blue sky. Despite their name, many floaters tend to sink toward the bottom of the eyeball, depending on the orientation of the eye. For example, when lying supine (looking upward), floaters may concentrate near the fovea, the central point of vision, making them more apparent against a textureless, evenly lit background. While floaters are common and usually harmless, they can be a significant nuisance for individuals with severe cases, especially if the floaters constantly drift through the central field of vision. The shadows cast by floaters are caused by tiny structures of protein or cellular debris trapped in the vitreous humor over time. Floaters can even be seen with closed eyes on bright days when sufficient light penetrates the eyelids to cast shadows. Although floaters are more common in older individuals, they can also affect younger people, particularly those with myopia (nearsightedness). They are also frequently observed after cataract surgery or eye trauma and, in some cases, may be congenital. Floaters can refract light in ways that temporarily blur vision until they move to a different location. They may also create the illusion of seeing something out of the corner of the eye that is not actually present. Over time, most individuals learn to ignore their floaters, but for those with severe cases, the large masses can be nearly impossible to disregard, leading to difficulties in concentration during activities such as reading, watching television, walking outdoors, or driving, especially when fatigued. Causes of Floaters Floaters can arise from various causes, all of which involve the introduction of material into the vitreous humor. The most common causes include: Vitreous Syneresis The most frequent cause of floaters is the shrinkage of the vitreous humor, a gel-like substance composed of 99% water and 1% solid elements. The solid portion consists of a network of collagen and hyaluronic acid, with the latter retaining water molecules. Depolymerization of this network causes the hyaluronic acid to release its trapped water, leading to liquefaction of the gel. The collagen network breaks down into fibrils, which become the floaters observed by the patient. Floaters caused by vitreous syneresis are typically few in number and linear in form. Posterior Vitreous Detachment and Retinal Detachment Over time, the liquefied vitreous body loses structural support, and its framework contracts. This process can lead to posterior vitreous detachment (PVD), where the vitreous body separates from the sensory retina. During this detachment, the shrinking vitreous can mechanically stimulate the retina, causing the patient to perceive random flashes of light across the visual field, often referred to as flashers. The complete release of the vitreous may result in the appearance of a large floater, commonly in the shape of a ring, known as a Weiss ring. In some cases, the detachment process can tear part of the retina, leading to retinal detachment. This condition often causes bleeding into the vitreous, which appears to the patient as a sudden onset of numerous small dots moving across the visual field. Retinal detachment is a medical emergency requiring immediate attention, as it can lead to blindness. The appearance of flashes or a sudden increase in floaters warrants an ophthalmological evaluation. Regression of the Hyaloid Artery The hyaloid artery, which runs through the vitreous humor during fetal development, regresses during the third trimester of pregnancy. Its disintegration can sometimes leave behind cellular debris, which may contribute to floaters. Other Common Causes Patients with retinal tears may experience floaters if red blood cells are released from leaky blood vessels. Similarly, individuals with posterior uveitis or vitritis, as seen in conditions like toxoplasmosis, may experience multiple floaters and decreased vision due to the accumulation of white blood cells in the vitreous humor. Other causes include cystoid macular edema and asteroid hyalosis, the latter being an anomaly of the vitreous humor where calcium clumps attach to the collagen network. These clumps move slightly with eye movement but return to their fixed positions. Tear Film Debris Occasionally, the appearance of floaters is due to dark specks in the tear film of the eye. While technically not floaters, they appear similar to the patient. Individuals with blepharitis, meibomian gland dysfunction, ocular allergies, or contact lens use are particularly prone to this issue. Tear film debris can be differentiated from true floaters by observing the effect of blinking: debris in the tear film moves quickly with a blink, whereas floaters in the vitreous humor are largely unaffected. Diagnosis Floaters are often readily observed by a doctor using an ophthalmoscope or slit lamp. However, small floaters near the retina may not be visible to the examiner, even if they appear large to the patient. Increasing background illumination or using a pinhole to reduce pupil diameter may help individuals better visualize their own floaters. Tilting the head to allow a floater to drift toward the central axis of the eye can also make the fibrous elements more conspicuous. Treatment In most cases, no treatment is necessary for floaters. Severe cases may be treated with a vitrectomy, a surgical procedure that removes the vitreous humor. However, this procedure is typically not recommended for mild symptoms due to the risk of complications, including blindness. Over time, many individuals grow accustomed to their floaters, to the point where they may no longer notice them. Another treatment option is laser vitreolysis, in which a YAG laser is used to vaporize the floater into a less dense and less noticeable form. This procedure can be time-consuming, and its effectiveness varies. One study found laser vitreolysis to be a safe but only moderately effective primary treatment, conferring clinical benefit in one-third of patients.
